750.title: Sabha: Indraprastha
750.hook: a message from a dead father: Pandu, through Narada, asks his son to perform the Rajasuya
750.howItsDone: Hindu families honor their ancestors in shraddha rites, with offerings of food and water, and in the season of Pitru Paksha, when the ancestors are remembered together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the halls of the gods, as Narada described them in Yudhishthira's sabha: each one known by who sits there. Did you widen the frame on something? Day seven hundred fifty.

Yudhishthira has been listening closely. And he's noticed something. In the hall of Indra, among all the sages and gods, Narada named only one human king: Harishchandra. Not the great kings of Yudhishthira's own line, not the heroes of the old stories. One name. Why him? the king asks. What did he do? And there's a second question, the one underneath. In the hall of Yama, among the dead, you saw my father. You saw Pandu. What did he say?
screen: `ONE KING IN INDRA'S HALL.` → `WHY HARISHCHANDRA?` → `AND MY FATHER?`

segments.voice: Narada answers the first question first. Harishchandra, he says, was a mighty king who brought other kings under him and then performed the great sacrifice called the Rajasuya. He gave generously to everyone who came. And because of that sacrifice, he shines in Indra's hall. Then the second answer. Narada had seen Pandu in Yama's hall, and Pandu had seen Harishchandra's place. So Pandu gave Narada a message to carry. Tell my son, Pandu said: you are able to conquer the earth, and your brothers obey you. Perform the Rajasuya. Then I, and our ancestors, may go to Indra's world. Sit with that for a moment. Yudhishthira's father died when the brothers were young, back in the forest. He has been gone for this whole long serial. And now, in the brand-new hall, in front of everyone, a sage turns and delivers his words. Not comfort. Not, I'm proud of you. A request, and a heavy one. There's something tender in it, though. Pandu is still thinking of his sons, and still thinking of his own fathers before him. The message runs both ways down the line. A son is asked to do something for a father, so that the father can rise with his ancestors. And notice how it reaches him: not as a dream, not as a ghost, but through a guest in the sabha. The hall that was opened by feeding people is now the place where the dead can speak to the living. Tomorrow, Narada adds something to the message that isn't nearly as welcome.
screen: `HARISHCHANDRA'S SACRIFICE.` · `PANDU SAW IT FROM YAMA'S HALL.` · `TELL MY SON: PERFORM THE RAJASUYA.` · `A FATHER, A SON, THE ANCESTORS.` · then, large: `THE DEAD SPEAK IN THE SABHA.`

segments.voice: Go gently with this one. Settle the breath. Bring to mind a parent, a grandparent, or an elder, living or gone, and something they hoped for you. It might be large or small, spoken or never quite said. You don't need to agree with it, or act on it. Just let it be heard, the way Yudhishthira hears his father's words. If you pray, you can hold that person in mind as you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Sabha. A hall, and its assembly. Today, in Yudhishthira's sabha, a sage carries a message from his father among the dead.
Your line: Sabha: Indraprastha. Today, pass on a kind word someone said about another person, to the person it was about. Day seven hundred fifty.

751.title: Sabha: Indraprastha
751.hook: Narada adds a warning to Pandu's request and leaves; everyone says yes, and Yudhishthira sends for Krishna
751.howItsDone: Hindu tradition remembers Krishna in the Mahabharata as a counselor as well as a god, and his advice to the Pandavas is often retold alongside the story of the Rajasuya.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a father's words in the sabha: Pandu, through Narada, asking his son to perform the Rajasuya. Did you pass on a kind word? Day seven hundred fifty-one.

Narada has one more thing to say before he goes. This sacrifice, he tells the king, is hard to finish. It has many obstacles. Brahma-rakshasas, demons who haunt sacrifices, look for any flaw in it. And after it, a war can come, one that destroys the warriors of the earth. Think it over, Narada says. Do what's good for you. And then he leaves, and the hall is left holding both halves of the message.
screen: `HARD TO FINISH.` → `DEMONS LOOK FOR FLAWS.` → `A WAR CAN COME AFTER.`

segments.voice: Put the two halves side by side. A dead father asking his son to rise to this. A sage warning that it might end in ruin. Yudhishthira doesn't brush either one aside. The text says he sighed, and thought, and couldn't find peace. So he does what a king in a sabha is supposed to do. He asks. First his ministers and his brothers. They all say the same thing: you deserve this, the time is right, do it. Then he asks the priests and sages around him, Dhaumya, and Vyasa himself. They agree too. Everyone in the room says yes. And still Yudhishthira doesn't move. The text gives his reasoning. People who love you, he thinks, don't always point out the danger. Some say what pleases. Some are carried along by their own hopes. So he thinks of one person who sees further, who won't flatter him, and who knows the world: Krishna. He sends a fast messenger to Dwaraka, and Krishna comes, quickly, to Indraprastha. So a unanimous yes doesn't end his asking. Yudhishthira isn't looking for a no. He's looking for someone who will tell him the truth, either way. A sabha, after all, is a room full of counsel. The best use of it is knowing whose counsel you most need. This is the last day of the hall's own story, the sabha at Indraprastha. Everything from here leans toward the sacrifice. Tomorrow, Krishna gives his answer, and the Rajasuya begins to take shape.
screen: `A REQUEST AND A WARNING.` · `EVERYONE SAYS YES.` · `LOVE DOESN'T ALWAYS SEE DANGER.` · `SEND FOR THE ONE WHO SEES FURTHER.` · then, large: `A UNANIMOUS YES IS NOT AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow. Bring to mind a decision in front of you, large or small. Notice who has already told you yes. Then ask yourself, quietly: who would tell me the truth about this, even if it isn't what I want to hear? Let a face come. You don't have to call them. Just know who it is, and breathe with that. The bell holds the time.
Sabha. A hall full of counsel. Today, every voice in it says yes, and the king still sends for one more.
Your line: Sabha: Indraprastha. Today, before you settle something that matters, ask one person who won't simply agree. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

752.title: the Rajasuya
752.hook: Krishna arrives, hears the plan, and names the one king who stands in the way: Jarasandha of Magadha
752.howItsDone: The Rajasuya belongs to the Vedic royal rites; in the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira's Rajasuya is the rite through which other kings recognize his rule at Indraprastha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day in the sabha at Indraprastha: everyone said yes, and Yudhishthira sent for Krishna anyway. Did you ask someone who wouldn't just agree? Day seven hundred fifty-two.
screen: `SEND FOR THE ONE WHO SEES FURTHER.`

segments.voice: Krishna comes straight from Dwaraka. Yudhishthira greets him, and lays the whole thing out. My father's wish. The sacrifice. My ministers say yes, my brothers say yes. But you'll tell me the truth. Should I perform the Rajasuya? And Krishna does tell him the truth. You have every quality it takes, he says. And then comes the but. There's a king in Magadha. While he lives, this can't be done.
screen: `KRISHNA COMES.` → `SHOULD I DO THIS?` → `YES. BUT THERE'S A KING IN MAGADHA.`

segments.voice: First, what Yudhishthira is asking for. The Rajasuya is the great royal sacrifice, the one Harishchandra performed. A king who completes it is honored by other kings as sovereign over them. So it can't be done alone. Other rulers have to come, and bow, and bring gifts. That's exactly the problem Krishna names. His name is Jarasandha, king of Magadha. In Krishna's telling, many kings already bow to him. And he has done something worse. He has captured kings in battle and holds them shut up in his mountain city, meaning to offer them as a sacrifice to Mahadeva. While those kings sit in his prison, Krishna says, no one else can claim to be honored by the kings of the earth. Krishna doesn't tell this from a distance. He tells it as someone who's been hurt by it. Fearing Jarasandha, he says, my own people, the Yadavas, left Mathura and went to live at Dwaraka. That's a striking thing for Krishna to say out loud. He's not posing as untouchable. He's telling the king plainly what this enemy cost his own family. And look at what his counsel actually does. It doesn't say yes, and it doesn't say no. It changes the question. Yudhishthira asked, should I perform the sacrifice? Krishna answers: first, what about the kings in that prison? The Rajasuya, in Krishna's hands, stops being a ceremony for one king's glory. It becomes a road that runs through a locked gate. Before anyone can be honored, someone has to be set free. Tomorrow, Yudhishthira hears that, and very nearly gives the whole thing up.
screen: `A SACRIFICE THAT MAKES A SOVEREIGN.` · `JARASANDHA OF MAGADHA.` · `KINGS LOCKED IN HIS CITY.` · `KRISHNA'S PEOPLE LEFT MATHURA.` · then, large: `FIRST, SOMEONE HAS TO BE SET FREE.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle into its own pace. Bring to mind something you want to do or build. Hold it lightly. Now ask, the way Krishna does: what stands in the way? Not to talk yourself out of it. Just to see the road honestly. Maybe there's something that has to be cleared, or someone who needs help, before the thing itself can happen. Let it show itself, and breathe beside it. The bell holds the time.
The Rajasuya. The great royal sacrifice that makes a king sovereign over kings, and that Krishna says can't happen while Jarasandha holds kings captive.
Your line: the Rajasuya. Today, pick one goal and name, honestly, the one thing standing in its way. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

753.title: the Rajasuya
753.hook: Yudhishthira wants to give the sacrifice up; Bhima and Arjuna argue for it, and Krishna tells how Jarasandha was born in two halves
753.howItsDone: The story of Jarasandha's birth is told in the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, which Hindus read, hear recited and see performed as part of the epic.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya ran into a locked gate: Jarasandha of Magadha, and the kings in his prison. What stood in the way of your goal? Day seven hundred fifty-three.

Yudhishthira hears about Jarasandha and does something unexpected. He backs down. If even Krishna's people fled from this man, he says, how can we stand against him? Let's give up the sacrifice. Peace is better. It's a startling thing to hear from the man whose father asked for this. Then his brothers speak, one after the other. And then Krishna tells a story about how Jarasandha came to be born.
screen: `LET'S GIVE IT UP.` → `THE BROTHERS SPEAK.` → `KRISHNA TELLS A BIRTH STORY.`

segments.voice: Bhima speaks first, and bluntly. A king who never makes an effort, he says, gets worn down like an anthill. Then he offers a plan: Krishna's wisdom, my strength, Arjuna's skill. Together, the three of us can do this. Arjuna argues too: they have the strength and the weapons, he says, so why hold back? Yudhishthira's caution isn't mocked. It's answered. And then Krishna tells where Jarasandha came from. There was a king of Magadha named Brihadratha, with two wives and no son. A sage, Chandakaushika, gave him a single fruit to bring a son. The king divided it between his two wives, so that neither would be left out. Each queen gave birth to half a child. One eye, one arm, one leg each. Horrified, the queens had the halves left outside. A rakshasi named Jara found them, and as she picked them up, the halves joined into one strong child. She gave him back to the king. And the text says plainly that his name comes from her: Jarasandha, the one joined by Jara. Why tell this now, in a war council? The story slows down to show who the enemy is before anyone fights him. And it isn't only a monster's tale. A father who wouldn't leave either wife out. Two mothers who couldn't bear what they saw. A rakshasi who, instead of harming the child, carries him home. Even the enemy has a family story. Tomorrow, the three set out for Magadha, and they don't go dressed as warriors.
screen: `AN ANTHILL WEARS DOWN.` · `ONE FRUIT FOR TWO QUEENS.` · `TWO HALVES, JOINED BY JARA.` · `EVEN THE ENEMY HAS A FAMILY STORY.` · then, large: `THE ONE JOINED BY JARA.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go on its own. Bring to mind a time you wanted to give something up because it looked too big. Notice what helped, or would have helped: a plan, a friend, someone who saw your strengths more clearly than you did. Let that person or that plan come into view. If it's still in front of you, you might picture the next small step, just one. The bell holds the time.
The Rajasuya. Today, the sacrifice nearly given up, then taken back up, with a plan and a story about the enemy's birth.
Your line: the Rajasuya. Today, when someone wants to quit, answer their caution instead of mocking it. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

754.title: the Rajasuya
754.hook: Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna walk into Jarasandha's city dressed as snatakas, refuse his welcome, and name themselves at midnight
754.howItsDone: A snataka is a student who has completed Vedic study and taken the ritual bath that ends it; Hindu tradition sets out a snataka's conduct, which is why Jarasandha notices that his guests don't look the part.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya almost given up, then Jarasandha's birth: two halves, joined by Jara. Did you answer someone's caution? Day seven hundred fifty-four.

Three men walk into the capital of Magadha wearing the dress of snatakas, young brahmanas who've just finished their studies. They have garlands on, and sandal paste. They don't come in by the main gate, which is a strange way for students to arrive anywhere. And they walk straight into the king's presence. Jarasandha stands up to receive them as honored guests. He has no idea that Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna are standing in his hall.
screen: `DRESSED AS SNATAKAS.` → `NOT BY THE MAIN GATE.` → `THE KING STANDS TO GREET THEM.`

segments.voice: Jarasandha does everything a good host should. He offers water, honors, a seat. And they won't take it. Krishna speaks for the group. My two companions, he says, are keeping a vow of silence until midnight. Then they'll speak. So the king leaves, and comes back at midnight, and now he asks the questions he's been holding. Snatakas don't usually wear garlands and paste like this. Your arms are marked like the arms of men who draw bows. You came in by a wrong way. And you refused my worship. Who are you? Krishna's answer is careful, and it's honest. A snataka, he says, enters a friend's house by its gate, and an enemy's house by another way. And we don't accept worship from an enemy. Jarasandha is puzzled. I've never wronged you, he says. Then Krishna names the wrong. You've captured kings and mean to offer them up as a sacrifice. We've come to free them. And he tells the king exactly who they are. Notice how strange this is. The disguise gets them through the door. But once they're inside, they don't hide why they came. They refuse the welcome. Some readers say that accepting it would have made them guests, and a guest can't rightly fight his host. They wait until he asks. Then they tell him their names and their reason. Jarasandha answers just as plainly. I took those kings in war, he says, and I won't let them go out of fear. Fight me, one of you, or two, or all three. He looks the three of them over, and he chooses Bhima.
screen: `THEY REFUSE THE WELCOME.` · `MIDNIGHT: WHO ARE YOU?` · `A FOE'S HOUSE, ANOTHER WAY IN.` · `NAMES AND REASONS, PLAINLY.` · then, large: `HE CHOOSES BHIMA.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a hard conversation you've had, or one that's coming. Notice what you're carrying into it. Is anything disguised? Is there a welcome you'd be accepting that you don't mean to keep? Picture saying your reason plainly, the way Krishna does at midnight. You don't need to say it to anyone yet. Just let it be clear to you. The bell holds the time.
The Rajasuya. Today it runs through Jarasandha's hall at midnight, where three guests refuse his welcome and tell him why they've come.
Your line: the Rajasuya. Today, if you disagree with someone, say your reason plainly, once, without dressing it up. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

755.title: the Rajasuya
755.hook: Bhima and Jarasandha wrestle for days and nights; the captive kings walk free, and Jarasandha's son is put on his father's throne
755.howItsDone: In traditional Indian wrestling, kushti, wrestlers train in an akhara, and Hanuman and Bhima are honored there as patrons of strength.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya's road ran through Jarasandha's hall at midnight, where three guests refused his welcome and gave their names. Did you say a reason plainly? Day seven hundred fifty-five.

Jarasandha does one thing first. He has his son, Sahadeva, installed as king. Whatever happens next, Magadha won't be left without a ruler. A king who holds other kings in chains still makes sure his own people will have someone on the throne. Then he takes off his crown, binds his hair, and steps out to meet Bhima. No armies. No weapons. Two men, bare-handed, and a crowd of citizens gathering to watch. The prison doors hang on how it ends.
screen: `HIS SON MADE KING FIRST.` → `NO ARMIES, NO WEAPONS.` → `BHIMA AND JARASANDHA.`

segments.voice: They wrestle, the text says, without stopping for food or rest, day and night, for days on end. They grip and throw. They strike with arms and knees. And then, at last, Jarasandha grows tired, and pauses. Krishna sees it, and speaks a word to Bhima, and Bhima takes it as his signal. He lifts Jarasandha high, whirls him around, and brings him down, and the king of Magadha dies. Here's where the story could turn into a conquest. It doesn't. The three go straight to the prison and open it. The captive kings walk out. And they turn to Krishna and ask, what can we do for you? Krishna's answer is small, almost polite. Yudhishthira wants to perform the Rajasuya, he says. Help him. That's all. Then something smaller happens. Jarasandha's son, Sahadeva, comes out with his ministers, bowing low, offering gifts. The kingdom is theirs for the taking. Krishna gives it back. He reassures the young man, and installs him as king of Magadha, on his father's throne. Remember where Krishna's counsel pointed at Indraprastha: before anyone could be honored, the kings in that prison had to go free. Now look at the order of what he actually did. Free the prisoners first. Ask them for nothing but help with a rite. And leave the defeated king's family their home. The Rajasuya is still to come. But here is one picture of what the rite is for, in Krishna's hands.
screen: `DAY AND NIGHT, BARE-HANDED.` · `JARASANDHA TIRES, AND FALLS.` · `THE PRISON OPENS.` · `THE SON GETS THE THRONE.` · then, large: `FREE THEM FIRST. GIVE THE THRONE BACK.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle. Recall a time you came out ahead of someone: an argument, a contest, a deal. Picture what you did next. Was there something you could have left them, or given back? There's no need to grade yourself. Just notice where the moment after winning sits in you. If you pray, you can hold that other person in mind for a few breaths. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
The Rajasuya. Today, its road opens a prison, and asks the freed kings only for their help, and hands a fallen king's throne to his son.
Your line: the Rajasuya. Today, when you win something, leave the other side something real. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

756.title: the Rajasuya
756.hook: the four younger brothers ride out to the four directions; in the far north, Arjuna reaches a land with nothing to conquer
756.howItsDone: The word digvijaya, conquest of the directions, outlived the epic: tradition uses it for the travels of the teacher Shankara, whose victories are told as debates won across India rather than battles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya's road went through a prison door: the kings freed, and Jarasandha's son put on his father's throne. Did you leave someone something real? Day seven hundred fifty-six.

Back at Indraprastha, the plan gets bigger. If kings are going to come and honor Yudhishthira, the brothers will have to go and meet them first. So the younger four divide the world. Arjuna rides north. Bhima rides east. Sahadeva rides south. Nakula rides west. Yudhishthira stays home, in the hall, with Dhaumya and his friends around him. Each brother will come back with the tribute of kings. And one of them will come back from a place where there was nothing to win.
screen: `NORTH, EAST, SOUTH, WEST.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA STAYS HOME.` → `A PLACE WITH NOTHING TO WIN.`

segments.voice: The text follows each brother in turn: kingdoms, battles, and kings who submit or welcome them and send gifts. It's a long march, told region by region. But one moment at its northern edge stands apart. Arjuna rides on, past mountain after mountain, until he reaches the land of the Northern Kurus. At the gate, powerful guards stop him, and they speak to him kindly. You can't conquer this place, they say. There's nothing here to fight. Even if you came in, you couldn't see anything with human eyes. We're pleased with you. Tell us what you want. And Arjuna doesn't push. He doesn't try the gate. He says, simply: I want my brother Yudhishthira to be sovereign. If this land is closed to humans, I won't enter. Give something as tribute, and I'll go. They give him fine cloth, ornaments and skins, and he turns back. Set it beside the battles around it. The conquest of the directions is about winning recognition for one king. And at the far edge of it, Arjuna, who won Draupadi with his bow, meets a land he can't win, and is content to ask. Now look back over this week. A father's message through Narada. A sage's warning, and a king who wanted honest counsel. Krishna naming Jarasandha. A birth in two halves. A midnight meeting, a long fight, a prison opened, a throne given back. And now the brothers coming home from four directions with the world's gifts. Everything is ready. Tomorrow, the Rajasuya itself.
